title: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
subtitle: Percentages · 10 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **10 of the official questions in Percentages are this one** — 1 Easy, 5 Medium, 4 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question has no real computation to do.
- It asks which expression shows increasing (or decreasing) a quantity by p%, or it says 'the new value is k times the old value, what is k?', or 'the value is the product of the base and r, find r'.
- The choices look like 0.p, p, 1.p, and 1 − 0.p.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) An increase of p% means multiplying by (1 + p/100).
- A decrease of p% means multiplying by (1 − p/100).
- 2) Pick the choice that matches the multiplier.
- If the multiplier is written as a fraction, simplify it.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: To check, give the variable a value like x=100 and compare what each choice gives against the value you expect after the change.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You pick the bare rate (0.p) or the percent as a whole number instead of 1 + rate.
You also might pick the decrease multiplier when the question says increase.
The distractors are exactly these, one per mistake.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You pick the bare rate (0.p) or the percent as a whole number instead of 1 + rate.
